Charles Lindbergh. The aviator who made the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight and became the world's first modern celebrity. On May 20th and 21st, 1927, Lindbergh piloted the Spirit of St. Louis, a single-engine Ryan Monoplane, across the Atlantic from New York to Paris in thirty-three and a half hours. He competed for the Orteig Prize, a reward of twenty-five thousand dollars that had been offered since 1919. Throughout the exhausting flight, he navigated by celestial observation and dead reckoning, fighting sleep the entire way. Lindbergh became the first living person to be widely recognized worldwide, a fame that set the modern template for celebrity. After landing, he toured the United States, promoting commercial aviation and encouraging its rapid expansion. He later married aviator Anne Morrow, who became a pioneering pilot and author in her own right. Lindbergh's accomplishment inspired other pioneering aviators like Amelia Earhart, who followed his transatlantic route five years later. His innovations built upon the principles established by the Wright Brothers, who made powered flight itself possible. Later in life, however, his reputation was damaged by isolationist views and his admiration for Nazi Germany during the nineteen-thirties.
